newsitem.title: USA: Guessing game on future of US ethanol tax break.
newsitem.headline: Guessing game on future of US ethanol tax break.

text.p: As House and Senate conferees meet this week to hammer out a tax bill, it's a guessing game on what the future will be for the ethanol tax break.

Senate tax legislation would extend the subsidy for producers of the corn-based fuel until the year 2007, paring it down modestly in that period. The House bill would leave the subsidy intact but end it as scheduled in the year 2000.
The National Corn Growers Association said it has the support in Congress to win an extension through the year 2007.
"We're just going full board for the Senate provision," said spokeswoman Ellen Dougherty.

But a farm group lobbyist, who asked not to be identified, said it appeared the most likely outcome for ethanol would be a three or four year extension in the tax break but at a lower rate, a middle ground between House and Senate plans.

And another agricultural analyst, who asked not to be named, predicted ethanol might be scrapped from both bills and the issue taken up later in the year in transportation legislation. President Clinton has proposed extending the tax break in his highway transportation bill.
Earlier Tuesday, House tax conferees agreed to send their Senate counterparts a first offer, which would not include any changes in the ethanol provision in the House tax bill.

"We have not gotten to that stage of debate yet," said House Ways and Means Committee spokesman Ari Fleischer. "But there is no possibility of the chairman accepting any proposal to continue and expand the ethanol tax credit" past 2000.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, Texas Republican, has been a staunch critic of the ethanol subsidy. Originally, his tax bill called for reducing the tax break and then eliminating it in the year 2000. He changed the provision in response to protests from other lawmakers.

Analysts said it will take intervention from top Republicans such as House Speaker Newt Gingrich of Georgia forthe Senate provision to prevail. This may happen, they said, if Archer's position hurts Republicans in farm country.

Currently, energy companies get a tax credit of 5.4 cents per gallon when they blend ethanol with gasoline. The ethanol tax break is worth billions of dollars a year to farmers. About five percent of the U.S. corn crop is used to produce ethanol.
